doc.title: Chuck Israels interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 11, 2021

title: Humphrey Lyttelton's tribute and Israels' melodic bass style
summary: Rowe reads Lyttelton's 1965 praise; Israels downplays virtuosity, stressing melodic playing, with Pettiford and Red Mitchell as models.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: That’s true. It’s true absolutely. Music is something that is very hard to pin down but people try. In fact I found this rather odd quote, Humphrey Lyttelton wrote it in 1965. He did a show called “Jazz 625.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
Oh, we’re on it. There’s all those —

Right. And he said, “Chuck Israels is a superb technician who handles the double bass as easily as if it were a guitar. He’s one of the reasons why musicians have come away reeling from performances by the Bill Evans Trio in a mood poised between elation and utter despair.”

Well he gives me too much credit for virtuosity. Well too much — it’s how he saw it. It was his perception of it. And maybe the perception of some other people. From my perspective, knowing my limitations in terms of virtuosity and technical prowess I think I used my abilities efficiently and perhaps — and I was a lot faster than I am now too, but that’s just — that’s true. I was fast enough for the music. And faster than, but mostly it was melodic, a melodic perspective about what you could do on the bass. I tried to play tunes when I wasn’t the only one doing that you know Oscar Pettiford did the same thing and Red Mitchell was the virtuoso who made all of us look silly. He was really superb. He was like Lester Young or Charlie Parker on the bass it was just gorgeous, incredible invention and freedom.
